1	// Pure pricing + guardrail math for CUSTOM VPS / game-server specs — servers
2	// bigger than the biggest premade plan ("Max"). No DB, no server-only imports:
3	// this is the ONE formula shared by the client-side deploy wizards (instant price
4	// as a slider moves, no round trip) and the server-side quote/order path
5	// (lib/custom-plan.ts, which re-validates everything here before a Plan row is
6	// ever created — a client-computed price is never trusted for money).
7	//
8	// ─── WHY "CUSTOM" EXISTS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9	// The premade ladder tops out at Max (4 vCPU / 16 GB / 120 GB). A customer who
10	// needs more than that on ANY dimension gets a one-off Plan row sized exactly to
11	// what they asked for (see lib/custom-plan.ts createCustomPlan) instead of being
12	// turned away or overpaying for a fixed "XL" tier that's still too small. So a
13	// valid custom spec is, by definition, Max-or-bigger on every dimension and
14	// STRICTLY bigger on at least one — never a way to buy something Max-sized (or
15	// smaller) at a different price, which would undercut the catalog and break the
16	// price-monotonic / disk-monotonic invariants lib/resize.ts depends on to keep
17	// upgrades honest.
18	//
19	// ─── PRICING FORMULA DERIVATION ──────────────────────────────────────────────
20	// The live ladder (prisma — Plan table) and its price DELTAS between adjacent
21	// tiers:
22	//
23	//   Tier      vCPU  RAM(GB)  Disk(GB)  Price      Δ vCPU  Δ RAM  Δ Disk  Δ Price
24	//   Starter     1      2        25     $8.88
25	//   Standard    2      4        50    $12.99        1       2      25    411¢
26	//   Pro         3      8        80    $20.99        1       4      30    800¢
27	//   Max         4     16       120    $32.99        1       8      40   1200¢
28	//
29	// A pure 3-variable linear fit (price = a·Δvcpu + b·Δram_GB + c·Δdisk_GB) across
30	// those three deltas turns out to be OVER-determined in a way the real ladder
31	// can't satisfy exactly: solving any two of the three delta-equations for
32	// (a, b, c) and checking against the third leaves a residual (405¢ vs 800¢ i.e
33	// disk-GB deltas here are exactly `20*Δvcpu + 2.5*Δram_GB`, so the three price
34	// points don't sit on a single consistent (a,b,c) — there's no clean 3-variable
35	// exact solution, only a best fit). So rather than force an unstable joint
36	// regression across three highly-correlated columns (cpu/ram/disk all grow
37	// together tier-to-tier), we ANCHOR the disk rate to a number the platform
38	// already charges for exactly this resource — `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`
39	// (lib/disk-expand.ts / lib/settings.ts), the live $0.10/GB/month a customer on
40	// ANY premade plan already pays to add root disk beyond their plan's included
41	// amount. Reusing it here means a GB of disk costs the same $ whether it comes
42	// from the extra-disk upsell or from building a custom plan — one number, one
43	// meaning, platform-wide.
44	//
45	// With disk fixed at that rate (10¢/GB), each tier-to-tier price delta minus its
46	// disk contribution attributes the REMAINDER to cpu + ram:
47	//
48	//   Standard-Starter: 411 - 10·25 = 161 = 1a + 2b
49	//   Pro-Standard:      800 - 10·30 = 500 = 1a + 4b
50	//   Max-Pro:          1200 - 10·40 = 800 = 1a + 8b
51	//
52	// Least-squares fit of those three (a, b) equations (normal equations
53	// 3a+14b=1461, 14a+84b=8722) solves EXACTLY to a = 11, b = 102 — i.e. $0.11 per
54	// extra vCPU/month and $1.02 per extra GB RAM/month. (RAM dominates the ladder's
55	// price growth far more than CPU does, which matches lib/capacity.ts's own
56	// framing of RAM as "the scarce resource" the platform oversells carefully
57	// while CPU is comparatively cheap to add.)
58	//
59	// All three rates are admin-tunable via lib/settings.ts (`custom_plan_per_vcpu_cents`,
60	// `custom_plan_per_ram_gb_cents`; disk reuses the existing `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`)
61	// so the catalog can be retuned without a redeploy if the premade ladder ever moves.
62	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_RATES: CustomPlanRates = {
63	  perVcpuCents: 11,
64	  perRamGbCents: 102,
65	  perDiskGbCents: 10, // mirrors extra_disk_gb_price_cents's shipped default
66	};
67	
68	/** Sane platform-wide ceiling — deliberately generous (nothing in the premade
69	 *  catalog approaches this), but not infinite: a real physical node has to be
70	 *  able to hold it. Admin-tunable via lib/settings.ts (custom_plan_max_*). */
71	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_CEILING: CustomPlanCeiling = {
72	  maxCpuCores: 32,
73	  maxRamMB: 128 * 1024,
74	  maxDiskGB: 2000,
75	};
76	
77	/**
78	 * The `sortOrder` every one-off custom `Plan`/`GamePlan` row is created with (see
79	 * lib/custom-plan.ts). Shared here — a pure, dependency-free constant — so
80	 * lib/order.ts and lib/game-order.ts can recognize "this specific row is an
81	 * intentionally-inactive custom one-off, not a retired/disabled plan" without
82	 * either of them importing the DB-touching lib/custom-plan.ts. See the doc
83	 * comment on their `active` gates for why this matters: a custom plan is created
84	 * `active: false` so it stays invisible to the 30+ existing `where: { active: true }`
85	 * catalog/marketing/resize-picker queries across this codebase (none of which are
86	 * scoped to a single order or customer) — but it must still be a valid PURCHASE
87	 * TARGET for the one order that just built it.
88	 */
89	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_SORT_ORDER = 999;
90	
91	export type CustomPlanSpec = { cpuCores: number; ramMB: number; diskGB: number };
92	
93	/** The floor a custom spec must clear on every dimension — today, the live "Max"
94	 *  plan's specs (see lib/custom-plan.ts customPlanFloor, which reads it from the
95	 *  DB rather than hardcoding it, so a future catalog change is picked up live). */
96	export type CustomPlanFloor = {
97	  cpuCores: number;
98	  ramMB: number;
99	  diskGB: number;
100	  priceCents: number;
101	  bandwidthTB: number;
102	};
103	
104	export type CustomPlanCeiling = { maxCpuCores: number; maxRamMB: number; maxDiskGB: number };
105	
106	export type CustomPlanRates = { perVcpuCents: number; perRamGbCents: number; perDiskGbCents: number };
107	
108	/**
109	 * The custom-plan price: Max's price plus the per-unit rate for whatever exceeds
110	 * Max on each dimension. Only the EXCESS over the floor is charged for — a spec
111	 * that matches Max on RAM/disk but asks for double the CPU pays only for the
112	 * extra CPU, not a second copy of Max's whole price.
113	 *
114	 * Defensively clamped to STRICTLY more than the floor's price: a valid spec
115	 * (per validateCustomPlanSpec) always exceeds the floor on at least one
116	 * dimension, so with positive rates this clamp is a no-op — but if an admin ever
117	 * zeroes a rate (e.g. sets `extra_disk_gb_price_cents` to "0"), a disk-only
118	 * custom spec must still never price at-or-below Max, which would silently
119	 * undercut the catalog (the exact class of bug lib/resize.ts's price-monotonic
120	 * guard exists to prevent one level up, at resize time).
121	 */
122	export function computeCustomPlanPriceCents(
123	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
124	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
125	  rates: CustomPlanRates,
126	): number {
127	  const extraCpu = Math.max(0, spec.cpuCores - floor.cpuCores);
128	  const extraRamGB = Math.max(0, (spec.ramMB - floor.ramMB) / 1024);
129	  const extraDiskGB = Math.max(0, spec.diskGB - floor.diskGB);
130	  const raw =
131	    floor.priceCents +
132	    extraCpu * rates.perVcpuCents +
133	    extraRamGB * rates.perRamGbCents +
134	    extraDiskGB * rates.perDiskGbCents;
135	  return Math.max(Math.round(raw), floor.priceCents + 1);
136	}

138	/**
139	 * Guardrails: every dimension must be at or above the floor (never a way to buy
140	 * something Max-sized or smaller under a different name) and at or below the
141	 * admin-configured ceiling. A spec that matches the floor EXACTLY on all three
142	 * dimensions is rejected too — that's just Max, not a custom order.
143	 */
144	export function validateCustomPlanSpec(
145	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
146	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
147	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
148	): { ok: true } | { ok: false; reason: string } {
149	  if (!Number.isFinite(spec.cpuCores) || !Number.isFinite(spec.ramMB) || !Number.isFinite(spec.diskGB)) {
150	    return { ok: false, reason: "Invalid configuration." };
151	  }
152	  if (spec.cpuCores < floor.cpuCores || spec.ramMB < floor.ramMB || spec.diskGB < floor.diskGB) {
153	    return {
154	      ok: false,
155	      reason:
156	        `A custom server can't go below ${floor.cpuCores} vCPU / ${floor.ramMB / 1024} GB RAM / ${floor.diskGB} GB disk ` +
157	        `on any dimension — for anything smaller, pick a plan above instead.`,
158	    };
159	  }
160	  if (spec.cpuCores > ceiling.maxCpuCores || spec.ramMB > ceiling.maxRamMB || spec.diskGB > ceiling.maxDiskGB) {
161	    return {
162	      ok: false,
163	      reason:
164	        `Custom servers top out at ${ceiling.maxCpuCores} vCPU / ${ceiling.maxRamMB / 1024} GB RAM / ` +
165	        `${ceiling.maxDiskGB} GB disk — contact support for anything larger.`,
166	    };
167	  }
168	  if (spec.cpuCores === floor.cpuCores && spec.ramMB === floor.ramMB && spec.diskGB === floor.diskGB) {
169	    return { ok: false, reason: "That's exactly the Max plan — choose Max above instead of building custom." };
170	  }
171	  return { ok: true };
172	}

174	/** Clamp an arbitrary (e.g. slider-dragged, or player-count-derived) spec into the
175	 *  floor..ceiling range, rounding to whole units. Used by the UI so a slider or a
176	 *  recommendation can never even VISUALLY suggest an invalid spec. */
177	export function clampCustomPlanSpec(
178	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
179	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
180	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
181	): CustomPlanSpec {
182	  return {
183	    cpuCores: Math.min(ceiling.maxCpuCores, Math.max(floor.cpuCores, Math.round(spec.cpuCores))),
184	    ramMB: Math.min(ceiling.maxRamMB, Math.max(floor.ramMB, Math.round(spec.ramMB))),
185	    diskGB: Math.min(ceiling.maxDiskGB, Math.max(floor.diskGB, Math.round(spec.diskGB))),
186	  };
187	}

189	/** Human name for the one-off Plan/GamePlan row this spec becomes. */
190	export function customPlanName(spec: CustomPlanSpec): string {
191	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
192	  return `Custom ${spec.cpuCores} vCPU / ${ramGB} GB / ${spec.diskGB} GB Disk`;
193	}

195	/** Slug pattern mirrors the one pre-existing manual precedent ("custom-4c8g-hmcebh")
196	 *  — short enough to stay under adminSavePlan's 30-char slug cap even at the
197	 *  ceiling's largest specs. `suffix` is a short random string the caller supplies
198	 *  (lib/custom-plan.ts) so this module stays free of any randomness/DB concerns. */
199	export function customPlanSlug(spec: CustomPlanSpec, suffix: string): string {
200	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
201	  return `custom-${spec.cpuCores}c${ramGB}g-${suffix}`.slice(0, 30);
202	}

content.thinking:
I realize the custom plan floor is VPS Max, so sliders like Minecraft's player count will always clamp upward to that tier—meaning custom is really meant for needs bigger than the standard ladder. I should keep that backend logic and just message it clearly: "Starts at X — for anything smaller pick a plan above."

On the security side, capacity gets rechecked at quote, confirm, and deploy stages, and pricing is always server-computed from the formula rather than trusted from the client, so guessable custom plan IDs aren't exploitable since the price floor is enforced server-side regardless.

One gap worth flagging: repeated confirm calls could spam orphan Plan rows since there's no rate limit in actions-custom-plan. I'll note it for the caller to decide on.

4	 * promo (longer commitment = cheaper); tune here (or later via admin Settings).
5	 */
6	
7	export type VpsTerm = { months: number; label: string; short: string; discountPct: number };
8	
9	/** The ANNUAL term is 12 months — the one term whose discount is admin-configurable. */
10	export const ANNUAL_TERM_MONTHS = 12;
11	
12	/**
13	 * The annual (12-month) commitment discount SHIPPED as the default, and the fallback
14	 * for the `annual_discount_percent` admin setting (lib/annual-discount.ts).
15	 *
16	 * It MUST equal the 12-month `VPS_TERMS` discountPct below: a platform whose
17	 * `Setting` table has no `annual_discount_percent` row must price the annual term
18	 * EXACTLY as it did before the setting existed, so no existing annual server's
19	 * renewal price moves the moment this wiring lands. The setting only ever raises or
20	 * lowers it deliberately, from the admin Billing panel.
21	 */
22	export const DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT = 20;
23	
24	export const VPS_TERMS: VpsTerm[] = [
25	  { months: 1, label: "Monthly", short: "1 mo", discountPct: 0 },
26	  // Annual is admin-configurable — this is only the SHIPPED default. Every charge
27	  // path resolves the live rate via `annualDiscountPct()` and passes it through
28	  // `vpsTermPriceCents`; this constant is what an un-wired caller (and a 2-arg call)
29	  // falls back to. Keep it === DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT.
30	  { months: 12, label: "Annual", short: "1 yr", discountPct: DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT },
31	  // Biennial/Triennial are FIXED platform rates (NOT admin-configurable), so for these
32	  // terms the order and every renewal read the SAME constant here → displayed ===
33	  // charged === renewed by construction, with no per-account freezing needed. Editing a
34	  // rate here only reprices NEW orders; any existing longer-term account simply renews
35	  // at the new (always-cheaper) rate — never an overcharge.
36	  { months: 24, label: "Biennial", short: "2 yr", discountPct: 30 },
37	  { months: 36, label: "Triennial", short: "3 yr", discountPct: 40 },
38	];
39	
40	export function vpsTerm(months: number): VpsTerm {
41	  return VPS_TERMS.find((t) => t.months === months) ?? VPS_TERMS[0];
42	}
43	
44	/**
45	 * The discount percent to apply to a term.
46	 *
47	 * For the ANNUAL (12-month) term this is admin-configurable: pass the
48	 * `annualDiscountPct` resolved from the `annual_discount_percent` setting
49	 * (lib/annual-discount.ts) and it WINS over the shipped default. Every other term
50	 * keeps its fixed `VPS_TERMS` rate. Omitting the override — or passing a
51	 * non-finite value — falls back to the shipped default, so a 2-arg
52	 * `vpsTermPriceCents` call and any caller that has not been wired up price annual at
53	 * `DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT`, i.e. exactly what the platform shipped before.
54	 * Clamped to 0..90 here as a second line of defence behind the setting reader.
55	 */
56	export function termDiscountPct(months: number, annualDiscountPct?: number): number {
57	  if (months === ANNUAL_TERM_MONTHS && annualDiscountPct != null && Number.isFinite(annualDiscountPct)) {
58	    return Math.min(90, Math.max(0, annualDiscountPct));
59	  }
60	  return vpsTerm(months).discountPct;
61	}
62	
63	/**
64	 * Total charge (cents) for a plan over a term, discount applied.
65	 *
66	 * `annualDiscountPct` (optional) overrides the ANNUAL term's discount with the
67	 * admin-configured rate; see `termDiscountPct`. It is the ONE knob that makes
68	 * annual billing configurable while keeping this the single price formula —
69	 * displayed (deploy wizard), charged (lib/order.ts) and renewed (renewalCharge)
70	 * all call this with the SAME resolved rate, so they cannot disagree.
71	 */
72	export function vpsTermPriceCents(monthlyCents: number, months: number, annualDiscountPct?: number): number {
73	  const pct = termDiscountPct(months, annualDiscountPct);
74	  return Math.round(monthlyCents * months * (1 - pct / 100));
75	}
76	
77	/**
78	 * Generic term price — the product-agnostic name for the ONE term formula above.
79	 * Shared Hosting, Business Email, Game servers and NxCloud all price a term as
80	 * `monthlyCents × months × (1 − annualDiscount)` exactly the way a VPS does, so
81	 * they call THIS and there is a single arithmetic for every product+term. It is a
82	 * thin alias of `vpsTermPriceCents` on purpose: the annual discount is resolved
83	 * once (order) and re-resolved (renewal) against the SAME setting, so
84	 * displayed === charged === renewed holds for every product.
85	 */
86	export function termPriceCents(monthlyCents: number, months: number, annualDiscountPct?: number): number {
87	  return vpsTermPriceCents(monthlyCents, months, annualDiscountPct);
88	}
89	
90	/**
91	 * The terms offered on the NON-VPS products (Shared Hosting, Business Email, Game
92	 * servers, NxCloud): the full ladder — Monthly, Annual (admin-configurable),
93	 * Biennial and Triennial — the SAME set VPS sells. Every product prices a term
94	 * through the one `termPriceCents` formula, so the longer-commitment discounts
95	 * (20 / 30 / 40%) apply uniformly across the platform.
96	 */
97	export const PRODUCT_TERMS: VpsTerm[] = [...VPS_TERMS];
98	
99	/**
100	 * Clamp any term input from a product order form to a SUPPORTED product term —
101	 * one of the `PRODUCT_TERMS` months (1 / 12 / 24 / 36). A malformed / unlisted
102	 * value can therefore only ever fall back to the cheapest (monthly) term, never
103	 * grant a longer paid term the customer did not pay for. The order path then prices
104	 * whatever term this returns through `termPriceCents`, so the charge always matches
105	 * the term granted.
106	 */
107	export function normalizeProductTerm(months: unknown): number {
108	  const m = Math.round(Number(months));
109	  return PRODUCT_TERMS.some((t) => t.months === m) ? m : 1;
110	}
111	
112	/**
113	 * Effective monthly-equivalent price after the term discount (for "$/mo" display).
114	 *
115	 * `months <= 0` returns the undiscounted monthly price rather than dividing by it.
116	 * This is not display hygiene — it is a money guard. `prorateDeltaCents`
117	 * (lib/proration.ts) prices BOTH halves of every upgrade and downgrade credit
118	 * through this function using `Server.termMonths`, and a 0 there made the division
119	 * `0 / 0` → NaN, which sails through `Math.round`, through `Math.max(0, delta)`
120	 * (NaN is not > 0, so the clamp returns NaN, not 0) and into `debitWallet` as the
121	 * amount to take. The result is a charge that either explodes at the database or,
122	 * on the credit side, writes NaN where a customer's balance used to be. The column
123	 * defaults to 1 and every writer clamps to >= 1 today, so this is a latch, not a
124	 * live bug — but a shared money function must not have a NaN in it.
125	 */
126	export function vpsEffectiveMonthly(monthlyCents: number, months: number, annualDiscountPct?: number): number {
127	  if (!Number.isFinite(months) || months <= 0) return Math.round(monthlyCents);
128	  return Math.round(vpsTermPriceCents(monthlyCents, months, annualDiscountPct) / months);
129	}

Small per-unit rates like 11¢/vCPU format fine as "$0.11". Now I'm sketching the builder component structure in CustomServer.tsx, defining a plan config type and components for selectable plan tiles and the custom builder itself.

For wiring into order.tsx, I'm planning to have the OrderProvider track extra custom plans and tiers in state, then merge them into the base catalog with a memoized computation. The context needs functions to add a custom plan or tier, plus a way to expose the current custom config through the Catalog type so the page can pass it through. I'm also deciding that if a user builds a second custom plan, it should replace the previous one rather than stack them.

I'm marking custom plan and tier options with an optional flag so existing logic like seedOrder and chooseGame naturally skip or handle them correctly since they lack recommended flags and typically have higher prices. For pricing, since custom plans won't be in the priceMatrix, I'm deciding to render the custom tile separately rather than forcing it through the shared pricedPlans mapping logic.

Now I'm working out that the custom plan tile needs its own confirmed/selected state showing the spec and current-term price, keeping it filtered out of the main pricedPlans grid. I realize storing a single effectiveMonthlyCents at confirm time would go stale if the term changes later, so I should instead store a full termMonthlyCents map on the PlanOption and merged category so the price recalculates properly when the term switches.

For consistency, game custom tile shows monthly pricing like other game cards, while the VPS custom tile shows term-effective pricing like PlanCards, both pulling from termMonthlyCents in the quote. For the builder UI, clicking the custom tile toggles a full-width builder panel below the grid, and if a custom plan is already confirmed, clicking it selects that plan and reopens the builder for edits — mirroring how PlanCard selection auto-advances but requiring an explicit confirm step for custom plans.

Now I'm sketching the builder panel itself: a header introducing "Build a custom server" with context about pricing above the largest plan, then a left column of sliders — starting with a player-count slider for game plans that maps to recommended specs via recommendedSpecForPlayers, flagging when the recommendation exceeds the ceiling, followed by CPU and other resource sliders.

I'll round the recommended disk to the nearest step above the floor, then design the price column: a big custom-server total, a line-item breakdown for extra vCPU/RAM/disk over the base plan, a term note showing monthly-equivalent pricing, a capacity status indicator, and a validation message for when the spec matches the floor exactly.

The confirm button stays disabled unless the quote and capacity checks pass and match the current spec, with errors surfaced from the confirm call. Below that I'm adding a sales-contact card that highlights in amber when limits are exceeded, plus mobile stacking and a "recommended for ~N players" note tied to slider values.

For the contact link, I'm building a prefilled message summarizing the custom request (product, players, spec, and any limit notes), URL-encoding it into a `/contact?topic=custom&message=...` link, and updating the contact page to read and validate those search params, passing them into ContactRoutingForm as initial values.

Then I'm noticing the pixel-identity category buttons would need a 6th entry, which actually fits better in a 2-column grid than the current uneven 5. Also flagging that the custom-tier display name for VPS/game plans gets ugly when concatenated with vCPU/RAM/disk specs plus game name — worth cleaning up the label format.

I want to override the injected GameTier's display name to something cleaner like "Custom · 8 vCPU / 32 GB" without touching the underlying DB name. In the PaymentSlide summary, I should add proper spec lines for game tiers too — CPU/RAM/disk plus a "Recommended for ~N players" line — so slots aren't presented as a limit, while bandwidth stays plan-only.

I also need to update the "Size your server" help text to emphasize memory and CPU as the deciding factors, framing player counts as recommendations rather than caps, and tweak GameTile's label from "{N} players" to "Sized for ~{N} players". Then I should search the Nexion wizard components for any other places "slots" is referenced to make sure everything is consistent.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# Part VII — Change history

Everything below this line is **history**, not reference. It is kept because the *reasons* recorded in
these entries are often the only surviving explanation for why a piece of code looks the way it does.
Where an entry contradicts Parts I–VI, **Parts I–VI win** — they were verified against the tree; these
were written at the time.

## How to read the change history

```
 Part VII is ordered oldest → newest in three layers:
   1. "Change history — the first 28 commits"   the compressed early record
   2. dated / titled entries                    one H2 per shipped change
   3. "Session log — 2026-07-26/27"             the most recent waves
 Authoritative alternatives when an entry looks stale:
   git log --date=short --pretty='%h|%ad|%s'
   git blame <file> -L <start>,<end>
```

## Session log — 2026-07-26 into 2026-07-27 (the customer-readiness push)

Seven commits, newest first. This document was last verified at `4ea9790`; everything above it in this
table is what the current pass folded in.

| Commit | Subject | Verified state |
|---|---|---|
| `2d8fedd` | Game servers renew at their game-plan price, not the base VPS plan | **Real.** `renewalQuote` delegates to `renewalCharge` and owns no arithmetic; a test asserts the file contains none. The extraction of `lib/renewal-charge.ts` was forced by a bu
| `f28f15e` | Refuse truncated Stripe metadata; one quote per order; honest receipt | **Real.** `packMetadata` throws before `checkout.sessions.create`; the sold price rides in metadata; the receipt attaches an invoice or points at billing history, never promi
| `3aa24d7` | Verification gates, auth lockouts, email verification (gate ships OFF) | **Mixed by design.** The two auth lockouts and the NAT flush are genuinely fixed. Email verification is **complete and deliberately disarmed** — `email_verification_enforc
| `7490131` | Stop charging customers without consent; card-save UI | **Real.** Three launch blockers from `docs/QA-JOURNEY.md`, all reproduced in a browser and all byte-identical in production, plus the card-save UI that had been wrongly marked complete |
| `156b6ac` | Harden the post-cutover TLS sweep against its own first live run | **Real, and verified on the live queue** rather than asserted: jobs drain, the permanent path settles, notifications stopped climbing |
| `4ea9790` | Promo-basis proration, post-cutover TLS, 8 more migration defects | **Real.** `Server.termPromoPercent` makes the proration round trip net zero by construction; the TLS pass stopped being dead code; 4 rows backfilled from real billing records wit
| `fd71056` | Migration rehearsal fixes, proration symmetry, wallet floor, CI | **Real.** Nine engine defects, the `capMonths` asymmetry, the sub-Stripe-floor card leg, and the first CI workflow |

The through-line across all seven is the defect this codebase keeps producing in new places: **a second
definition of something that already had one.** A second renewal formula. A second promo basis. A
second place `lastAutoBackup` could be written. A second email-normalisation. The fix, every time, was
to delete the duplicate rather than to make the two agree.

input.message:
**Done.** The custom-server option and "Talk to sales" path are built into the Nexion deploy wizard for both VPS and game servers, and player counts are now shown as recommendations. Committed as `47eee7428d` on `feat/game-plans-custom`, with explicit paths only. The commit includes a docs §15 entry in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`. `npx tsc --noEmit -p .` is clean. I walked both flows with Playwright on staging (sandbox mode) at 1440 and 390, up to the Payment step, never paying. The dev server on port 3034 is stopped (killed by PID; the port is free).

**What was built**
- **Custom card and builder** (new file `components/nx/CustomServer.tsx`). A "Build your own / Custom" card sits beside the plan cards (VPS) and the tier cards (game). The card says "from $X/mo", where X is the cheapest real custom build. Clicking it opens a builder under the grid:
  - A "How many players?" slider for games. It sets recommended vCPU/RAM/disk from `lib/game-player-recommend.ts`. Its maximum is the lower of `playerSliderMax` and the top of the game's own max-players setting (e.g. 200 for Minecraft).
  - vCPU, RAM and disk sliders, held between the floor (the top active plan, Max: 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 120 GB) and the admin ceiling.
  - An itemised price: the base price, plus each added resource × its rate, plus included transfer.
  - The number that moves with the slider is a client preview from `computeCustomPlanPriceCents`. "Use this custom server" only enables once `quoteCustomPlanAction` confirms price and capacity for exactly the spec on screen.
  - Confirming calls `confirmCustomPlanAction` / `confirmCustomGamePlanAction`. `OrderProvider` (`components/nx/order.tsx`, new `applyCustomPlan` / `applyCustomTier`) then adds the new plan to the session's catalogue and selects it. From there region, quote, summary and `payAndDeploy` / `payAndDeployGame` run exactly as for a normal plan.
- **Backend addition** (`lib/actions-custom-plan.ts`). The quote and confirm actions now also return `termMonthlyCents`: the per-term monthly rate, computed on the server with the live annual discount. That lets the custom card show term prices without the browser doing any maths.
- **Page** (`app/dashboard/deploy/page.tsx`). Passes `customPlan` (floor/ceiling/rates) the same way `legacy-page` did. The custom option hides itself if there is no base plan.
- **Talk to sales.** The builder always shows a "Talk to sales" card. It turns amber and becomes the main call to action in three cases: the player count needs more than the ceiling, a slider is at the self-serve max, or capacity is short. It opens `/contact?topic=custom&message=…` in a new tab, pre-filled with product, game, players, spec and term.
  - The contact form did support categories, so I added `custom` ("Custom / large server", routed to contact@) in `lib/contact-categories.ts`.
  - `lib/actions-contact.ts` now builds its allowed-category list from that same map.
  - The contact page reads `topic` and `message` on the server (message capped at 2,000 characters) and pre-fills `ContactRoutingForm`.
  - Side effect on the marketing contact page: the category grid now has 6 buttons instead of 5.
- **Player wording in the wizard:**
  - Game tiles say "Sized for ~N players".
  - Tier cards say "Recommended for ~N players".
  - A note under the tiers reads "No player cap from us — limited only by your server's resources and the game's own maximum."
  - Seeded tier names like "Minecraft — 2 GB / 10 slots" show without the "/ 10 slots" part (display only; the database is unchanged).
  - The Payment summary now lists the game tier's vCPU/RAM/disk and "Recommended for ~N players · no player cap from us".
  - For the game cap, the builder says "The server's max-players setting goes up to N". I deliberately don't call that an engine limit, because it's our own config setting.
- **Two mobile bugs fixed while verifying.** They existed before this change. At 390px the game Server-step card (fix: `min-w-0`) and the Payment grid, once the Stripe card field loads (fix: `grid-cols-1`), were wider than the screen.

**Server-side protection (checked).** A custom plan can't be bought below the floor or past a capacity check:
- `createCustomPlan` re-checks floor, ceiling and capacity when the plan is confirmed.
- The price comes from the stored plan row, not from the browser.
- At purchase, `placeOrder` re-runs the RAM and disk capacity checks, and `placeGameOrder` re-runs the RAM check (see gaps below).

**Screenshots**, in `/tmp/claude-0/-root/ec6fa978-d80b-4147-9982-eea470598e2c/scratchpad/wiz/`. Each exists at both widths as `1440-*` and `390-*`:
- VPS: `vps-1-plans`, `vps-2-builder`, `vps-3-at-max` (amber sales card), `vps-4-region-after-custom`, `vps-5-payment` (server-quoted $61.75 for 8 vCPU / 32 GB / 240 GB)
- Contact: `contact-prefilled`
- Game (Minecraft): `game-0-picker`, `game-1-tiers`, `game-2-builder`, `game-3-max-players`, `game-4-few-players` (the "fits our standard plans" note), `game-5-custom-selected`, `game-6-region`, `game-7-payment` (custom $41.35, specs and recommendation in the summary)

**What I couldn't do or verify**
- **Login:** the staging admin credentials in `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt` were rejected ("Invalid email or password"). I was blocked from looking up admin users in the staging database. Instead I made two throwaway customer accounts on staging through the normal `/register` form (`wizard-test-mujvl70x@example.com`, `wizard-test-mujvndln@example.com`). That credentials file needs refreshing.
- **Leftover staging rows:** each walk-through created several inactive one-off custom Plan/GamePlan rows (`sortOrder` 999, `custom-*` slugs) in `nxeon_staging`, a dozen or more in total. I didn't delete them because I don't have database access here; they're safe to remove.
- **Not exercised:** the "player count needs more than the ceiling" amber state for a game (Minecraft at 200 players stays under 32 vCPU / 128 GB). A failed capacity check wasn't exercised either. Both use the same code as the VPS at-max case, which was exercised.
- **Pre-existing, not fixed:**
  - Hydration error on `/dashboard/deploy?product=vps`: `seedOrder` builds a random default hostname inside a `useState` initialiser, so server and client render different names. This is the anti-pattern CLAUDE.md warns about.
  - `placeGameOrder` doesn't re-check disk capacity at purchase, for any game order. Custom game plans are disk-checked at confirm only.
  - The confirm actions have no rate limit, so repeated confirms create extra inactive Plan rows.
  - Other places still say "slots": `lib/marketing/gameLocationLandings.ts` ("up to N concurrent players"), `components/nx/Provisioning.tsx` ("Preparing N player slots"), `lib/nx/plan-specs.ts` ("N slots" in the services list), plus the seeded tier names themselves.

content.text:
The custom-server option is built into the Nexion deploy wizard for both VPS and game servers, and player counts now show as recommendations. It's committed as `47eee7428d` on `feat/game-plans-custom` (not deployed), and the typecheck is clean. I tested both flows on staging (sandbox, nothing charged) at desktop and phone width, stopping at the Payment step.

- **Custom card and builder:** a "Build your own" card sits next to the plan and tier cards, with a price starting just above the biggest plan. For games, a "How many players?" slider suggests vCPU, RAM and disk. Separate sliders then let the customer adjust each one within our minimum and maximum. The price is broken down line by line: the base price, then what each added resource costs.
- **Price and capacity checks:** the price updates as the sliders move, but the "Use this custom server" button only unlocks once the server confirms the price and that there's room. After that it goes through the normal region and payment steps like any other plan. The server re-checks the minimum, maximum and capacity when the plan is created, and again at purchase, so a custom plan can't be priced below the minimum or skip the capacity check.
- **Talk to sales:** the builder always shows a "Talk to sales" card. It turns amber and moves to the front when:
  - the player count needs more than our self-serve maximum;
  - a slider is at its limit; or
  - we don't have room right now.

  It opens `/contact?topic=custom` with the game, player count and spec already filled in. I added a "Custom / large server" category to the contact form for this, so the marketing contact page now shows 6 categories instead of 5.
- **Player wording:**
  - Game tiles say "Sized for ~N players".
  - Plan cards say "Recommended for ~N players".
  - A note under the plans reads "No player cap from us — limited only by your server's resources and the game's own maximum."
  - Plan names hide their "/ 10 slots" suffix in the wizard; the database names are unchanged.
  - For a game's own limit, the builder says "the server's max-players setting goes up to N". That number comes from our own config setting, so it doesn't claim to be a limit of the game itself.
- **Two phone-layout fixes:** at phone width, the game "Server" step and the Payment step were wider than the screen. Both were already broken before this change, and both are fixed.

**Things you should know:**
- **Login:** the staging admin login in `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt` was rejected as invalid, and I wasn't permitted to look up admin accounts in the database. I signed up two throwaway staging customers through the normal register page instead (`wizard-test-mujvl70x@example.com`, `wizard-test-mujvndln@example.com`). That credentials file needs updating.
- **Leftover staging data:** the test runs left a dozen or more inactive one-off custom plan rows in the staging database. They're safe to delete; I couldn't do it without database access.
- **Not tested:** the amber sales state for a game that's too big, and a real "no capacity" response. Both run on the same code as the VPS "at the limit" case, which I did test.
- **Problems I found but didn't fix:**
  - The VPS deploy page throws a hydration error, because it generates a random default hostname differently on the server and in the browser.
  - Game orders don't re-check disk space at purchase. This applies to all game orders; custom ones are checked when the plan is created.
  - Nothing limits how often someone can create a custom plan, so repeated clicks leave extra unused rows.
  - "Slots" wording still appears outside the wizard:
    - the game location landing pages ("up to N concurrent players")
    - the provisioning screen ("Preparing N player slots")
    - the services list ("N slots")
    - the seeded plan names in the database

Screenshots are in `/tmp/claude-0/-root/ec6fa978-d80b-4147-9982-eea470598e2c/scratchpad/wiz/`, as `1440-*` and `390-*` pairs. For example, `vps-3-at-max` shows the amber sales card and `game-7-payment` shows the custom game in the order summary.
